Early data shows new police team arresting more drug dealers on Salem streets

  • Madeleine Moore
  • November 13, 2026
Share on Facebook Share on X (Twitter) Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:48
Instaread

A new police team is showing initial promise by multiplying arrests made for drug deals happening on Salem streets.

For over a month, the Salem Police Department’s Drug Response Team has targeted people dealing drugs, while also offering to connect those using substances with services.

The team’s work is focused on enforcement and education. It aims to “root out” drug dealers preying on Salem’s vulnerable and unhoused communities, Interim Police Chief Brandon Ditto said.

Early data shows the team of two specialized detectives is making roughly four times the number of arrests compared to patrol officers.

“So far, we’ve been very happy with how they’re conducting business and making sure that it’s safety-related and cutting off those distribution networks, so people have a chance, right? Recovery,” Ditto said.

The team launched at the end of September as part of a city initiative announced earlier this year meant to address the presence and effects of drugs and substance use around Salem. The effort is part of a broader plan to respond to public concerns about safety and cleanliness.

The Drug Response Team, a pilot program, is planned to run until at least December 2027, according to Ditto. The team is backed by $216,342 from the city’s general fund, he said.

In just over a month, the team made eight arrests following investigations into drug dealing, according to Angela Hedrick, the police department’s initiatives manager.

Recently, patrol officers were averaging around two arrests per month for the same type of investigations, according to Hedrick.

The previous pace for drug distribution arrests was “quite a bit lower,” due to shifting enforcement focuses for the patrol force, Ditto said.

The department has a three-tier approach to tackling drug distribution in Salem.

The two detectives work at the street-level, while the department’s mid-level team handles statewide drug production and trafficking, including those selling to street dealers, Ditto said. There is also a detective working with the federal government on national and international investigations.

To Ditto’s knowledge, this is the first time the Salem Police Department has had a team focused on street-level drug activity.

When hiring for the team, the department wanted people with specialized experience in drug investigations. Due to Oregon’s decriminalization of drug possession in 2021, younger patrol officers had a gap in investigative knowledge when it came to those cases, according to Ditto.

“Obviously (it) was decriminalized, and that was all drugs across the board, so you had a whole segment of our patrol or incoming patrol force that weren’t well-versed in investigating drug crimes,” he said, referring to the short-lived Measure 110. “So when it’s criminalized again … let’s talk about search and seizure law, let’s talk about what levels of narcotics you would need for certain prosecution rates for distribution, delivery charges, things like that.”

The team uses complaints reporting drug activity to investigate local dealers, according to Ditto. They also use surveillance and talk with people in the community to learn about drug houses or other locations where there’s suspected dealing, he said.

So far, the team has seized 104 grams of fentanyl and 111 grams of methamphetamine, according to numbers Hedrick provided.

Just over a year ago, community members reported drugs and crime as the second most important issue through a city survey. The top issue from survey respondents was homelessness and poverty.

In response to growing public discussions around safety and cleanliness, the city launched two separate initiatives – one expanded the police team working at homeless camps and established a new crisis team for those with mental health and medical challenges.

The other initiative brought to life the drug team, which police leadership had been considering for more than a year, according to Ditto.

Started in March, the initiative set out to not only enforce the law for those dealing drugs, but to offer treatment to those using substances with services among community partners.

“For the dealers, there’s going to be enforcement measures, and that’s what their goal is, is to root out the dealers that are dealing to, especially the vulnerable populations we’ve seen in the community that are living outdoors, the unsheltered population, because unfortunately, a lot of the dealer networks are targeting those populations,” Ditto said.

One key partner for the new team is a program run by the Marion County Sheriff’s Office called Law Enforcement Assisted Diversion, or LEAD. The program, which started in 2018, has since become a reference for how to help people avoid prosecution for minor crimes while connecting them with recovery services.

Through LEAD, people can avoid being taken to court for low-level offenses if they work to address their underlying reasons for breaking the law, which are often homelessness and addiction.

For eight years, LEAD has succeeded in getting people to use drugs less, find housing and secure employment.

So far, the Salem Police team has connected one person to LEAD, according to Ditto.

In addition to the county program, the team is working with Bridgeway Community Health and a “vast network” of local partners in housing and healthcare, Ditto said.

“That’s the priority for any kind of users, any kind of treatment that we can get them into,” he said.

To measure progress, the department is tracking the number of contacts with those using or dealing substances, arrest warrants written, amounts of drugs seized and people connected with services, Hedrick said in an email.

When the team’s pilot year nears its end in December 2027, the city will “follow the data” on where resources are needed to decide whether to continue the team, Ditto said.
